title: Average (Arithmetic Mean)

references.label: GSSSB Laboratory Assistant Detailed Syllabus, Part A (Advt. 327/2025-26)

scientificNotes: General competitive-exam quantitative-aptitude topic; included to match the exam's Part A scope.
expression: Average = (Sum of all values) / (Number of values)    Average speed (equal distances) = (2 × S1 × S2) / (S1 + S2)
explanation: The average (arithmetic mean) is the sum of all observations divided by their count — it can shift substantially due to a single outlier, unlike the median. A classic exam trap is AVERAGE SPEED for a journey covered at different speeds over EQUAL distances (not equal times): the correct average speed is NOT the simple arithmetic mean of the two speeds, but the HARMONIC MEAN — because more TIME is spent travelling at the slower speed for the same distance, so the slower speed should (and does) pull the average down more than a simple mean would suggest.

variables.meaning: Two different speeds used to cover the SAME distance each way

workedExample.scenario: A car travels from A to B at 40 km/h and returns the same distance at 60 km/h. Find the average speed for the whole trip.
workedExample.result: Average speed = 48 km/h (NOT the simple mean, 50 km/h)

commonMistakes: Taking the simple arithmetic mean of two speeds for an equal-DISTANCE journey — the correct average speed formula for equal distances is the harmonic-mean-based (2·S1·S2)/(S1+S2), since unequal TIME is spent at each speed.

Forgetting that a new value added to a group changes the average by an amount that depends on how far that value is from the OLD average, not on the value itself in isolation — useful for 'find the new average after including one more term' problems.
genZNote: Average speed for equal distances isn't the polite middle-ground mean — the slower leg eats way more time, so it drags the average down harder than you'd expect.
